pages.text:
*The Seventeenth Rule of Mapmaking: Sign your work only when it is true.*

The last seven miles were a blur of mud and breath. They had borrowed a cart from a farmer who did not ask questions, but the wheel jammed on the third mile, and they pushed. Dumpling walked with the stubbornness of a mule who knows he is right about everything. Odd ran alongside, his red hair flying, his mouth open in a laugh that sounded like a hiccup. Tam clutched the map case to her chest. It was wrapped in oilcloth twice, heavy and slick against her ribs. Her lungs burned. The air tasted of wet stone and horse sweat.

Then the trees broke. The wall of Verrin rose before them, grey and solid against the sky. The bells began to toll. One. Two. Three. They ran the last stretch on foot, the cart clattering behind them. Tam’s boots slapped the cobbles. The crowd was already gathering, a sea of faces turned toward the Guild Hall. The smell of baking bread and wet wool filled the air. She could hear her own heartbeat, thumping against the oilcloth like a trapped bird.
pages.image: A muddy cart being pushed by a sturdy girl in a patched coat and a gangly boy in red, with a grey mule walking stubbornly beside them, approaching a tall grey stone city wall with church bells visible in the distance.

pages.text:
The Guild Hall was a cavern of polished stone, its white marble floor inlaid with a compass rose so vast that Tam had to wade across the northern arm just to find the needle's tip. Shelves climbed the walls, stacked high with rolled maps that resembled sleeping snakes, while the long table at the far end held twenty unrolled sheets glowing in the high window light. They were beautiful, indeed. Gold leaf shimmered, serpents guarded the coastlines, and colors bled into one another with a soft, perfect smoothness that made Tam’s hands itch.

The judges sat in a row, their dark robes swallowing their bodies until they looked less like people and more like shadows with elbows. At the center sat Guildmaster Aurelio Quint, tall and stately, his silver compass chain catching the light as he read from a scroll. His voice was deep and clear, cutting through the silence.

"Lucan Ravel," he called. A boy in a green coat stepped forward with his back straight as a ruler.
"Bram Hale. Ines Vane. Then..."

Quint paused. He looked up, scanning the crowded room with eyes that seemed to search for a specific smudge. "Tamsin Marrow?"

Tam stumbled into the room. Her knees were muddy to the top, her hair was full of reeds and twigs, and she was breathing like a bellows. The marble floor was clean, and she could see her own footprints, dark and wet, leading from the door to the table.
pages.image: A girl with mud-stained knees and messy hair standing in a grand hall with a marble compass floor, looking up at a tall man in dark robes at a long table covered with colorful maps.

pages.text:
Tam unrolled her map on the table. It was not beautiful. The ink was brown and black and grey, and the lines were thick. The compass rose was a wobbly circle that looked like it had been drawn by a hand that had been shaking. There was no gold leaf, and no serpents. In the corner sat a blot that looked suspiciously like a fish hook.

The hall went silent. It was a heavy quiet, the sort that settles over a room when a drop of water falls into a still pond. The Academy maps glowed beside hers, bright and perfect. Hers looked like work. Honest, tired, real work.

One of the judges leaned forward and squinted. He cleared his throat, making a sound like a dry twig snapping, while another judge leaned in to examine the blot. They did not look at the gold leaf.

At the back of the room, Lucan stood with his hands folded. He watched Tam. His face was smooth. He did not smile, and he did not frown. He simply watched, his eyes steady and bright.
pages.image: A judge leaning over a long table to inspect a simple, dark map with thick lines and a wobbly circle, contrasting with a bright, gold-leafed map next to it, while a boy in a green coat watches from the background.

pages.text:
Tam felt a presence in the corner and turned to find a wooden chair propped up on a stool, occupied by a figure wrapped in a lavender scarf. A white bun of hair stuck with pencils sat atop the head, and a hawthorn cane rested across the knees. Master Finch had come by cart, ignoring every piece of advice given to her. Her ankle was bandaged, swollen, and purple.

She did not wave, nor did she smile. She simply met Tam’s eye from across the vast, echoing hall. Then she nodded once, a small movement that spoke the language of one craftsman to another. It said, *I see you. I see the line. It is straighter than yesterday.*

Something filled Tam’s chest, expanding until it took up the whole room. It was not joy, and it was not pride, but a feeling that made the air inside her lungs feel solid and heavy, like a bag of wet sand. She swallowed, her throat dry, and looked at the map, then at Finch. She straightened her back, standing as tall as the ink on the page.
pages.image: An old woman with white hair and a lavender scarf sitting in a chair with a bandaged ankle, looking calmly at a girl across a large room, while a hawthorn cane rests on her lap.

pages.text:
Guildmaster Quint stood. The room hushed. He walked to the center of the table, his robes sweeping the floor with the soft thud of a heavy book falling on a desk. He looked at the twenty maps. He looked at the twenty apprentices.

"Each of you," he said, his voice low and serious, "will now explain how you made your map."

He paused. He looked at Tam, then at Lucan, then at the others. A hint of a smile touched his lips. It was a small thing, barely there.

"And also," he added, "how you improved in the making of it."

A murmur went through the hall. It started as a whisper and grew into a rustle. Heads turned.

In the corner, Master Finch closed her eyes. A smile spread across her face, slow and deep. It looked like she had just won a very long argument.
pages.image: A tall man in dark robes standing at a table, looking seriously at a group of young people, while an old woman in the background closes her eyes and smiles peacefully.
